analysis.one_liner: Taxes the US-bound profits of companies that manufacture goods offshore instead of in America.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 25, 2011 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax rules, a company can move its factories overseas, sell the goods back into the United States through a foreign subsidiary, and avoid paying US tax on those profits until the money is brought home. This bill would treat profits from goods made abroad and sold in the US as immediately taxable American income, with its own limit on credits for foreign taxes paid. It would take away the tax reward for offshoring production and keep manufacturing, and the tax revenue that comes with it, in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits: American factory workers and communities that compete against imported goods, domestic manufacturers that keep production here, and US taxpayers generally, because profits from goods sold in America would be taxed here instead of deferred offshore.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US factory workers and domestic manufacturers

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds 'imported property income' to the list of income that controlled foreign corporations must count as immediately taxable US income, covering profits from manufacturing, selling, leasing, or licensing goods made abroad and imported into the United States [S2][S3].

It reaches beyond a company's own imports: profits on goods a foreign subsidiary sells to unrelated importers who are expected to bring them into the US also count, closing a common routing scheme [S3].
It gives this income its own basket in the foreign tax credit rules, so companies cannot mix it with other foreign income to reduce what they owe [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that manufacture products in low-cost countries and import them for sale in the United States, including US-owned and foreign-owned companies alike; some of the added cost could surface in prices for imported consumer goods.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinationals manufacturing offshore for US sale

drawbacks.text: Companies facing a higher tax bill on imported goods may pass some of the cost to US consumers in the prices of imported products, and the bill's own text acknowledges exceptions where goods are re-exported or unavailable domestically [S3].

Splitting imported property income into its own foreign tax credit basket adds significant compliance complexity for companies with global supply chains, and raises the risk of disputes over what counts as 'reasonably expected' to be imported [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: the bill removes a tax advantage that currently rewards moving factories abroad, which would help keep manufacturing jobs and tax revenue in the United States. The cost, honestly stated, is that some of the tax burden on imported goods could show up in consumer prices, and the rules are complex to administer. On balance the bill is a direct attempt to end a subsidy for offshoring, though its heavy compliance machinery reflects how hard it is to tax global supply chains.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Whitehouse introduced the bill on January 25, 2011, joined at introduction by six other senators, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
Eight senators signed on as cosponsors, seven Democrats and one Independent [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the bill's entire recorded history is introduction and referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations that manufacture goods overseas and import them into the United States, which kept the current tax treatment of offshore production, along with the Finance Committee leadership that never had to take a position on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies making goods offshore for US sale

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 25, 2011 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters were Democrats plus Independent Bernie Sanders, and no Republican cosponsored; no vote was ever taken, so the full partisan split was never tested.

industries.industry: Multinational manufacturers producing abroad for US sale (consumer electronics, appliances, apparel and similar goods)
industries.note: These companies benefit from the current rule that lets profits on US-bound goods made offshore go untaxed until repatriated; the bill would tax that income immediately. Their gain under the status quo comes at the cost of US manufacturing jobs and federal revenue.

By taxing profits on imported goods the same as goods made in America, the bill removes the tax incentive to move production offshore, putting domestic production on more even footing with imported goods.

industries.industry: US companies with complex global supply chains
industries.note: The bill creates a new income category with its own foreign tax credit basket and a 'reasonably expected to be imported' test reaching third-party sales, adding substantial compliance and planning costs for companies whose supply chains cross borders.
